blocks.x: I'll make a note we're recording Mr. Eddie Marrero at 1822 Annette and the date is October the 11th 1961 this is Bill Russell. Do you mind giving your full name? Do you have a middle name?
Yeah Edward Joseph Marrero.
Edward Joseph huh? Yeah. Do you mind telling just when you were born, your birth date?
Yeah I'm born 1902 August the 4th.
So you were just a little bit younger than Lawrence is that right?
Yes a little younger than Lawrence.
You were born a year or so over there?
A year over me, between 11 months and a year.
I don't remember if Lawrence told us just what part of town you all were living in? Where did your father live?
Eickward down in Spain and Viry, 1327 Spain Street.
Spain and Viry.
Between Viry and Eickward.
Had your father lived there most of his life, that part of the town do you remember?
We lived around, years ago around Calorat and Claiborne.
It wasn't so far from there.
Then we moved down.
Then you moved down farther.
That's where he died at. Yeah.

I wonder if you can tell us, of course everyone knows that your father, Billy Marrero was a famous bass player. I wonder if you can tell us anything about him? About his family? Well, about him personally, when did he die? I don't even know how old he was when he died. Do you remember about him?
Yeah, he was 47 years old.
Only 47, that was.
No, no, no.
No issues.
No.

I'm going to ask again about your brother John we were talking about, that band that he played with the Bichets, and that was about 1916. You say Sydney wasn't very old and it just started out then with...
He was young. It just started out. He used to play flute. He started from a flute and somebody bought him old clarinet and he started playing clarinet and John was playing guitar.
Oh he played guitar, he started then on...
Good guitar. Good, good guitar.
When did he take up banjo about?
John took up banjo around in about 1924.
Not until later then.
Yeah, later. He used to play guitar, good guitar.
Yeah, no doubt. He could play banjo as well as he did. He must have been fine on the guitar too.
Yeah, he played guitar like a piano man.
How did he, did he pick with all of his fingers or just drum the whole thing?

No, he's... He could pick and rap at the same time. Yeah. Combination. Yeah, combination. I don't know, he hit the up stroke and the bottom stroke. I don't know how he done it but I used to see him do like this, you know.
Johnny St. Cyris already does that too. He has a six string banjo.

Well you see, yeah he played the guitar banjo. He never played a tenor banjo. He played the guitar banjo, the six string banjo. He still does. He still play that. Yeah. I remember when he left here with Louis Armstrong in there. Yeah, went to Chicago, that's right.
Went to Chicago, yeah.
When Louis, when Joe Oliver sent for Louis, for Louis. I played that dance out there at the fire ground. Oh yeah. But I played with Kid Rene.
Good luck, alright. How was he on the top? Oh, the greatest. I heard him in the late years when he, you know, he started sick and wasn't... He was going down, yeah.
He was going down, yeah.
He was going down I guess in those days, but I heard that in 1942, not I heard any of it.
We thought Freddy Keppert was good, but he was better. You liked him better.
Oh yeah.

That man could take a cornet. He'd be playing a number and go, go above the staff and stay there until he'd go out. I mean everything, keen and clad, nothing, nothing, nothing spoiled. Yeah. You know I'd pick up a cornet round right there.
Did you play with him wrong and just a few jobs?
No, I played with him a while when Simon was sick. Oh, alright. And everywhere they played I went on a job. So you're going to have to take him in and look.
Don't worry, don't worry. That won't matter. He can still hear you.
Everywhere I went on a job, I used to go expel Simon.
Yeah.
Well, otherwise I played the whole job most of the time. I liked to have to advertise him when I get on the truck and play the advertisement for him. Oh yeah.
Is there anything else you can tell about Simon? How he got started on base? Did your father help him? Did you tell us?

Well, he helped him in the later years. When Simon got started on base, we lived on Bourbon Street, Bourbon and Marais. He took one of those, I won't say soap boxes, but it was a, the thin stuff, but it was a milk can box. Yeah. Old Magnolia box. And they had a boy they used to call Albert Murphy. The old cheese box, the cheese used to come around. He made a drum out of that. Yeah, I see those, yeah. But Simon made a bass. That's how he started. Made his own instrument. Made his own instrument. And from then on, my daddy got him a little bass about a year after that.
How old do you suppose he was until then?
When Simon got started.
Before he started.
Simon would have been around about, about seventeen.
Oh yeah. And who did he play with first? Do you remember?
They didn't play with, just a bunch of boys in the neighborhood. Not knowing, none of them didn't come to be no musicians outside Simon and John. They all dropped out. Yeah.
They all dropped out.

Cause they had the little homemade cornets, you know, made out of little brass and this and that and things like that. But it was no instruments. Yeah. But you sing through them, penny parties they played for. Yeah. In the yard. Yeah, I don't know. Penny to go in.
But they had a lot of fun.
Oh yeah, it was plenty of fun.
Then do you remember who, which bands he played in? Simon we're talking about now. Simon? Sure.

Bands around New Orleans? Yes. Well, he started from Buddy. He went with Buddy. Oh, they must have stood together for about twelve years. And from Buddy, he went to Rene. Kid Rene band. Stayed with them in front of us? He stayed with them all, long time. And he left Rene with Celestan Tuxedo band.
John was with them then too, wasn't he? John was with them then.
They'd been trying to get them two together for years. They never could get them two to double.
Which one joined Celestan first, John? John.
John was assistant manager of the band.
So I thought he was, they always talk about John any time they mention Celestan.
Yeah, well he was better known than Simon on the county. He worked longer with Tuxedo band than Simon did.
Had John started in music earlier then? Did he start a little bit before Simon to learn his instrument and all of it? Why not?
No, he started a little before. John went to the country, Uncle Henry showed John what he knew. Simon was working for Ragman Lang then. That's true. On the furniture truck.
Oh yeah.
When John was learning to play guitar, Simon was working on the furniture truck.
Yeah.
Yeah, he started before Simon. He started a little bit before Simon.
And he joined Celestan after John got him in there? No.
Yeah, it was years after before he joined Celestan. So I mean he joined Celestan after John then?
John had already been in Celestan.

Yeah, John had been with, yeah it was Ridley Tuxedo band. Yeah, Ridley. They call it Celestan, but it was Ridley Tuxedo band. Ridley was really the manager. He was the manager and John was the assistant manager. Yeah, that's it. Then after Ridley and Celestan had a separation, so Celestan had his Tuxedo band and Ridley had Ridley Tuxedo band.
They had those two very well.

See they had two. So Simon went with one and John stood with Ridley and Simon stood with Celestan. You see? That's right. That's right. That same Barbaran. He's the one who tried to get Simon to go to New York at night.
Paul. Paul Barbaran.

The one who was talking to last night. Yes. He was playing with Louis Armstrong. Yeah, that's right, yeah. He was playing with Louis Armstrong. So Simon refused him and he had a little falling out. They did Simon to do a trickle. Simon wired him and next day when they went to the bank to get the tickets, Simon had his tickets and everything to go to New York.
Yeah.
That's how he went to New York with the Blue Rhythm Boys.
Yeah, I met with that other group. I never knew that he played up there with that group. I knew that John was up there. I never knew that Simon.
He went before John.
Yeah, he went even before John. Yeah.
He had went and come back and then left again with King Oliver band. Yeah.
And he was out on the road with that. I guess I heard that once probably Paul or somebody told us and I forgot about it. Well, Paul was in the band.
Yeah. Paul was the leader of the Oliver band.
I know he arranged the music and everything.
He arranged and everything. Paul was the leader of that band.
I guess he told us that Simon was there and I just forgot. Is there anything else? Did you ever play yourself a stand band? I guess you'd sit in sometimes.

I never, I sat in plenty. Like I told you with Simon taking sick for three months and I worked in his place. The whole time he was sick. He had rheumatism and he all swole up. He couldn't play his hands and all. Well, that's the whole time. I never did join his band. But I have worked for Ridley personally in his place on Howard between Drive and Barone. I used to take calls for the Tuxedo band when they come in, you know. I'd phone call. That was before I was playing. Even before you took out?
Yeah.
I was pressing.

Oh yeah, that's right. We talked originally a couple of times. It's been so long now I almost forgot what he said. That's why we take everything down on tape so we have it all down and all this information isn't lost. But he told us something about how the band split up and I don't remember all the details. About the band split up?
About the band split up.
Yes. So at least we, I think we have that information from Ridley too. He just died last year. Yeah, I was up there.
I saw y'all up there. At the funeral. Oh yes, that's right.
Way up in the car.
It was a big funeral at that time too. That's history of the old days.
Yes.
And this is for the Tulane History Department. History.

There's a lot of people, some days, they say they say they say they're not going to be more interested even than they are now and then so we try to talk to the musicians themselves and get the story straight because a lot of things have been written about it that come
on. There's plenty of things. You asked me something about Bung Johnson.
Oh yes.
He's a third corner player. My daddy's friend. He was the third and the next to the last. The last man was Sam Morgan. Sam Morgan was the last.
I knew Bung White well when he came back.
Bung first come from New Iberia and my daddy picked him up on Grabby and Ramport. Freddie first, Joala was second, and Bung Johnson.
And Bung Johnson. Yeah. How was Freddie Kemper? Did you hear him much?

I heard him a couple of times, not too much, but he was a, you know, corner player, he played something like, high up above the staff. Everything was high he played. He never was no sweet corner player. Yeah.
Bung was sort of a sweet.
Sweet. Oh yeah. Bung was a sweet something like Buddy and Lewis and those. All them had the tree and style because Buddy, I mean Bung, partly learned Lewis, Buddy Petit, everything he knew.
That's what Bung told me too, yes. Yeah.
He learned everything you know. He helped him. He helped him. He helped him. He helped Lewis too.

I know George Lewis once told me, I used to make records of Bung and George together, you know, and Lawrence, you know. Yeah. First one he told him, shh. I know George once said he put him behind the curtain, sometimes you couldn't tell Bung and Buddy Petit. That's right. That's the way they played.
He learned him. So he had that soft touch just like Bung, sweet below the staff.
Yeah.
Nothing above.
Yeah.
Just below. Yeah. That's the way they played going down.
Well, I think, is there anything else you can tell us about your father? You mentioned the three trumpets. Kepard was the first then. Was Kepard playing before Oliver? Do you remember?
He was playing in the same time, but he was playing with my daddy before Oliver.
Your daddy happened to hire him first.
Yeah. He was playing before Oliver. Yeah. Because he played with the Sapira band.
Do you remember who else worked with your father? Any other musicians around your home when you were boys?
One you might know. One used to play violin called Jimmy Palau. Oh, Jimmy Palau. He was in Chicago.
He was in the band.
No. I knew Daniel Perez.
I met him before he got hit.
And Richard Payne's guitar player.
Oh, yes. His guitar player.
His picture's on that. Walter Brennan, you know. Yeah. Richard Payne had a mustache.
I can't remember. Your father did, didn't he?
Yeah. Richard Payne had a mustache too today. He kind of favored my daddy. Yeah, that's right. Little short man, kind of favored him.
He looked a little something like him in that picture that I saw. Yeah. Yeah.
Well, that's the band I'm calling. Louis Nelson was playing Klein at. I knew him very well.
I made some records.
Well, he was playing in that time with that bunch. He played with the whole treatment. The Superior, the Imperial.
Do you remember where they would work? Did you ever hear your father say where they were going to go to work?
Well, most of the jobs they played, I heard them talk a hall I had never went in and never knew nothing about the Old Gloves Hall. Oh, yes.
Up by the basin. I never saw it.

I never heard it. I never saw it. I mean, I never saw it in that hall. Because I couldn't go up there and that day I was too young. And plenty danced down at the Farz Amir, the hall you mentioned. Yeah. Well, they hired their band all the time when they had a big to-do. Yeah. They had my daddy in them band. He had partly, or saw the white ground here.
Well, I think of it. Some people at times, I don't know if they just get mixed up, but they call your father Billy Moran or something like that. Yeah.
Billy.
Billy.
Moran. That's what they used to.
How did they just, didn't know any better?
Didn't know any better.
And I guess he just let them go.
He didn't correct them. That's the way. My brothers and them was the one that correct the name when they went to the plane, you see. And they called them Moran and they correct it.
Yeah, I just wondered if they just made a mistake.
Simon, Joan, and Lauren. Lauren. They correct the name right. Yeah, I knew Lauren.
Sort of a nickname. I knew Lauren very well, yeah. Yeah, he knew Lauren good. Yeah, since 1942 I met him. He's always dead. You know Papa.
You know my name?

No, I never knew him, no. No. I've heard so many people like Bunkin all talk about him that I feel like I know him. And knew Lauren and all, and the rest of the families too, you know, like the Frazers and Lauren and all, there's so many people. You didn't know John? Never knew John. No, he didn't know.
No, he didn't know.

And know R. Simon. And when I was in New York in 1940, 1930, or 1940 was it, I know Red Allen, I met him then, and he told me that another New Orleans musician, at that time I liked New Orleans music.
We're the one who gave me stuff.
And he told me that John was up there working at a drug store, I mean Liggett, something Liggett, something like that.
Liggett, a drug store.
I made a note of it, I was going to go up and try to see him and meet him and talk to him, I never did though.
Then I moved away from there that fall and he died. That's where he got killed then.
In an accident. When did he die? He died in 1942.
I left there in 1940, I should have seen him. I could have seen him if I had just gone up there. He's living right over the drug store.

Too bad, I always wanted, I had it on my list to go, but a lot of things I got in neglect and I'm always sorry that I didn't let him. At that time I hadn't even met Lawrence, so Lawrence was the first of the brothers that I met.
Yeah, well he got the best break out of all the brothers.
Yeah, in a way.
He's done all the, I mean everything fell in his favor, radio, television and all, but
he was a kid. Yeah, then he got sick there.
Simon took sick.
Simon had a con-brain to play with Kev Callowee, you remember that?
Yeah, we got that telegram. Yeah. What'd he done with it?
He was sick and he was sick.
Simon could have went off with Noble Sicilis. They wanted to swap places, my brother. Noble Sicilis bass player was a pure Frenchman.
Was he from here or any place?
Noble Sicilis?
No, I mean the bass player.
The bass player, no, he born and raised in France. In France, oh. You see, he wanted to bring his wife to the United States.
Yeah.

So Simon was playing at the Blue Rhythm Club. What he was going to do, play with the Blue Rhythm Boys, take over Simon's job, and Simon go overseas with Noble Sicilis. I mean he, and his wife will come over, bring his wife, I mean he's going to bring his wife over and take over Simon's job, you see?
By the way, speaking of the Blue Rhythm Boys, do you think Simon ever made any records with them? They made some in Lucky Melander.
Yeah, he must have made some records, when John made records.
When did Simon die? I don't know. Did you tell us, maybe you told us.
I don't remember. Yeah.
What year you mean?
Yeah, it's about one year.
Let's see, I'm going to keep right. Nellie, we got that down all in the book, you know. What year Simon died in? What year Simon died in?
What year Simon died in?
November 28, 1935.
November 28, 1935.
November 28, 1935.
I don't know what it was written. 1935.
That's far back, huh?

I was just wondering, I used to hear the Lucky Melander's Blue Rhythm Band, that was probably after that time. After that time, yeah. You hear him up in the Apollo Theater and all the other people, the Harlem Opera House a lot. So I guess your brother was dead then by that time. I don't think I heard him until about 1935 or 1936, along in the Depression, I know. I might have heard him before, but not.
But he had stopped playing before that. Well, he stopped.
Quite a while before that. No, I never heard him. No, I never heard him.
No. He was taking sick somewhere around in 1933.
No, I wouldn't have heard him. No. That's a big, 1935, 1936.
He's taking sick on Stucker's boat. The Macapalow out there.
Yeah, that's right.
They put him off in St. Paul, Minnesota and sent him here.
He was on the boat.
Yeah, he was on the boat plane and he was with fake marble.
Yeah.
That was his last job. With fake marble. Yeah.

Is there anything else about your father? I don't like to keep bothering you with all these questions, but I mean, if you can't tell us, there's no one else now left. Much that can never tell us about your father. What you mean? Did you ever practice around home then? Any bands come to your home when you were a boy to practice or what?
We used to get, we used to have to close our doors to keep the people out. Oh, yeah?
That's all they ever done.
Really?
All the music there was done.
That was twice and three times a week.
Really?

Music there was done. Music like Joliver and all them. Come home. Now you see, my daddy was a man who liked good fun. You see, on Mondays, he'd have a turtle dinner for all the musicians when it was downtown. A red bean dinner. Red bean and shortcake. He used to do that every Monday. What is a shortcake?
All I know is like strawberry shortcake. What did you call a shortcake in those days?
This one right there. You want to taste the piece of that?

Yeah, I don't want to. Don't bother to cut you. Let me look after that. Oh, that's okay. Wait, is it more just like a... Yes, sir. More like biscuit, the bread. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, like biscuit bread. Yeah. That's the kind my mother used to make and put strawberries on it sometimes. Oh, yeah. You call that shortcake just as well.
Shortcake. Strawberry cake.
You just eat it with butter or do you have other things on it? Yeah, I would, but...
It's good.
Mm-hmm. And you'd have those dinners then for the musicians, huh?
Yeah, every Monday. Every Monday. Every Monday. Every Monday. That's how we kept. Now, rehearsals, they have that twice and three times a week.
Yeah.

And you know how people hear music, how they would crowd around, they were white and colored. Yeah. Especially back in those days, we used to live neighborless, you know, with each other downtown. Yeah. Because the boys, they'd stay in my house, most of the time I'd sleep at his house and he'd sleep at mine.
Yeah. Yeah, I know in the old days it seemed to be a lot more friendly. Yeah.
People were somehow.
Yeah, it was friendly.
Yeah. Yeah.

Looked like they were pulling away from each other, right? Yeah, and everybody was suspicious of one another and everything. Yeah, yeah. It's terrible, so. So, was that his regular band that he'd have to meet there or just other people come in sometime to practice?
Any of them, any musician. Almost anybody come in and.
Any of them could fit in.
Mm-hmm. He'd have his regular band with some concert, like musicians and all. Yeah. They'd just go down in the rehearsal. Yeah.
Or something like that.

Yeah. Well, they'd go down and get happy, they'd pick up the horn. Yeah. Yeah. Or they'd take a, you know, olden days when a musician would go to the rehearsal, he'd take his instruments with him. Mm-hmm.
Yeah.

He didn't go along. Yeah. If he played clarinet, he took his box with him. If he played clarinet, he took his clarinet with him. If he played trammone, he took his clarinet with him. If he played band, guitar, he took his guitar with him.
Yeah. They always had their instruments.
Always carried their own instruments. That's the way they done it in the olden days. Yeah. You see. So, that was his fun. Shortcake, red beans, pick a poke meat.
Strong coffee.
That's a good time. We used to call that Blue Mondays.
Oh, yeah. Blue Mondays. Another thing I've heard that had dances sometimes like Economy Hall places on Monday nights, too. Is that a popular night to have dances?
Yeah, every Monday. Then he used to have the banquets, too. Yeah, I've heard of those.
Bonquets.
I played a couple of them. Yeah, they call them bonquets. I played a couple of them night ones. There were very few night ones there in my head.
They were in the afternoon and the evening. Early evening.
Yeah, and eating two o'clock from two to six. Yeah. Everything free. Yeah. Well, back in the 20's, man, they used to have hams that big, them baked hams. Yeah. You know, those baked hams.
Yeah, I remember singing when I was a kid, too.
Pickled ham, them pickled ham. Yeah. Ooh, them things was good. Yeah. Well, they'd give you all that. You're dance free. Yeah. Five, six, maybe eight kegs a beer, all that.
The club would put that on.
The club would put that on. The club would put that on the society. Yeah. And all that be free. All you had to do was get in there if you could get in.
Yeah.

A whole lot of people couldn't get in there. Really had a good time. Get in there, you see what I mean? Sure. There'd be more people outside than the inside. They'd be begging. They won't pay you to get in like that. So I got a many of them in for nothing. There's God. Sometime I'll get five and six of them in there at a banquet. That was good time.

I was going to ask a little more about the, the, the, the, the, the, the, the playing, actually playing the bass. I know you were over there at the Autocrat Club a couple of years ago when they were rehearsing with Lawrence and the Barnes Brothers and all. I guess just Paul was in it then. And you were talking about in the old days, we used to bow most of the time that even when you played, you used to bow a good deal? Yeah.
Bow a good deal. Such as waltzes, charlices, of course they don't play that.
No, they don't play the trunce. They still play the trunce.

Or you take a number when it first, you first, well most of the bands in those days didn't play the introduction of a number because half of them couldn't read good enough to do it. And the bands wasn't qualified enough to do it. But they was fab musicians. Yeah, they really played what they could play. Yeah, they played voice and chorus. But all right, we take the voice and the chorus. You start off with your bow. Then when the band get in between the numbers, you put your bow in between your hand and, you know, we picked it from the wrist like this.
You usually pick with the first two fingers?

First two fingers, you see, and again. Now they slap them like that. Yeah, slap the whole finger. Well you can't get the tone out the bass like that, I changed the most. You got to hit when you're fingering the bass. Make sure that it's down tight.
Tight. Yeah, the whole thing.
No rattle, no nothing, you know what I mean, or something like that. And when you hit them with these two fingers, well this finger have a cone here and a cone there.
I noticed I'd slow drag off with the tape on their fingers quite a bit. And they don't wear off the skin.

Well I never did tape on. After I was playing four months, I didn't need no tape. That's good in touch. The big blisters come on there and I wouldn't try to bust them. I wouldn't try to do anything. They turned the cones. And I kept on playing with them until they turned the cones.
I played violin, my fingers there pretty tough.
Oh yeah, right on there. Yeah, you see?
Pretty tough, yeah.
Get out to you, that banjo voice. See the banjo cut your right? Oh yeah, steel strings, yeah. That's why they're a fool with banjo.
Yeah, they're sharp.
I could learn banjo.

I don't know. I was going to ask about the three string bass in the old days. I know one time old man Glenny was playing a three string bass. Do you know if your father always played four strings? Four.
He always had four. Never played three. Never played a three. That's the advantage of over a tree, you see? You go to hit a pedal note below the staff, how you going to hit it? You got three strings.
Yeah, they leave off the lowest string. Yeah.

The low E string. That big E string, you take that off them, that's the main thing. A whole lot of people say, you see a man with three strings on his bass, you think he know what he's doing, but he don't. Yeah, I think so too. It's against him. See? But a four string bass, you're playing right. And a whole lot of people, when they learn them instruments, first thing they go to a teacher, instead of letting them show them the instruments, first before they try to learn how to play anything.
Yeah.

Know they want to learn to play any stuff more. They hear the key of B flat or C or F and they play in them three familiar keys, well they're satisfied. Then they're ready to work. When people start throwing them in them shops and things like that, they don't know what to do.
Yeah.
They don't know their next chord. See?

One of you, when you were young did you have any other favorite bass players, no doubt your brother and your father, of course I know they were great, but were there any other great players around that you liked?
One was Jim Little. Yeah, I heard him too.
And the other one was Albert Morgan. Oh yes, he's a young fellow though.
Me and him come together. We learn together. Simon learned both of us.
Is that right? I talked to him for a while out in California about three years ago. He could play. Yeah, I heard him play at times. He could play. He still plays out there. He's still playing.
He was the youngest one of the more. He was down here about two years ago.
Is that right? I didn't see him.
Yeah, he was down here about two years ago. He's one of the youngest Morgan brothers. He'd come after all of them. Yeah.
Did you say you played in the Morgan band, the Sam Morgan, like did you ever take a substitute or anything for Jim Little, or he was usually the bass player?
Well, yeah, when I walk in the dance. Yeah. You see, those fellows was the only band in the city didn't like for you to touch the instruments. Sam Morgan. And it was a regular routine with musicians.
Yeah.

If you come in the dance and you see the fellow playing, you play a guitar, you'll play a drum or something, you tell the drummer, let me rest you up. Yeah. You may play that two hours, an hour and a half. But Sam Morgan and them didn't like nothing like that.
Yeah.
No. They liked to stay to they self. They didn't want the bass player to let you play. He wouldn't let his brother play at all. I could play, but he wouldn't let his brother play. Really?
Wouldn't let the…
Wouldn't let Albert play. Wouldn't let Albert play. Run him off the music stand. Never would leave Albert play on any job. Albert never had the pleasure of playing with Sam Morgan band. I could.
Yeah, it's strange he wouldn't let his brother play. Like you say, some of them, I guess I thought it was a good rule to stick, for the whole band
to stick together. He oughta been glad to bring his brother out faster.
Yeah, you'd think so, yeah.
They helped him out. He was young. Yeah. Just getting learning, you know what I mean? Very good too.
I mean he had a lot of talent, but he wouldn't be as good as he is.
He's got plenty of talents. He's one of the best he is up there right now. That's right, no? I don't know if he's slipping out, but he's good. He's still good.
He's good.
Last time I was down here with Louis Jordan. He come down here with Louis Jordan. Yeah, he was a good, good man. He made the best musician out of all the Morgans.
Yeah, I guess in some ways he got to be more famous nationally all over the...
Then he liked that music. Yeah. You see, I mean.
Yeah. Played with any type of a band.

Any type of band he could play with. Yeah. He played with a cab a long, long time. And he jumped from cab and went with a other band. Albert could play any type of music. Yeah, that's right. Well, that's what made him actually good. Played with a six-piece band, or he could play with a sixteen-piece band.
Were there any of the other old-time players I even remember? Was that Jimmy Brown used to play with Manuel Perez? What was he like? Do you remember? Was it his... That was the...
Was he playing with Jimmy Brown?
That was the bass player.
Yes.
Do you remember what style he played?
He played on the style that they used to class him and my daddy about like that.
Really a good player.
He was good. Good, good, good. Old Man Kimmel, too. Oh, yeah.
That's right. He played on the boat, too, didn't he?
Yeah, Old Man Kimmel. Old Man Kimmel. Well, Jimmy Brown was extra good. I never knew him at all.
I've seen his picture, though.
Yeah, he was extra good-faced, bro. Jimmy Brown was good as any of them. But my dad had better name than him.
Yes, he was more famous as the manager of his own band.
Yeah, and managing famous bands. Yeah. That's what made him... You know, but Jimmy Brown was a good-faced, bro. Extra good.
Do you remember this, the Proudhon's... How was he? I never heard much about him.
Johnny Proudhon?
Yeah, he died long before I got to know him. Yeah, he been there.
Well, he was sort of a... Did you hear him as... Yeah, I used to be my good friend. He was the rough type.
More rough type.
Yeah, you know.
Not as good a musician.
Five-piece band or something like that. He just played what he thought was made, what he thought was right, and if it was wrong, and so on. Yeah. That's the kind of bass player he was. Oh, oh yes.

I have one of these, yes. I have one of these, yeah. It's nice. Looks just like it, all right, sir, too. Yeah, it's a nice issue. Yeah, I have... Thank you for showing it to me. There's only about a half a minute here. Anything else you'd like to add before we... There's something I want to add.
Yeah, anyone ever told you about Wooden Joe? Oh yes, I knew him.
You knew him? I knew him. I made records with him. Yeah. He was a kind of...
You played with him for a while.
I know Lawrence did.
Lawrence. Little Lawrence Toko. Yeah, Lawrence played with all of them. Yeah. He played with more bands than me. Oh yeah, I guess he... Because I gave up.
He played longer than you did then. Yeah, he played...
Oh, way long. He played over 30 years long. I don't know. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you.

segments.title: Opening and Eddie Marrero's birth
segments.summary: Recording intro at 1822 Annette on October 11, 1961; Eddie gives his full name and says he was born August 4, 1902, a bit younger than Lawrence.

segments.title: Father Billy Marrero's homes and death at 47
segments.summary: Eddie names the Spain Street house and earlier addresses near Claiborne; his father the bassist died at 47.

segments.title: Brother John's guitar and banjo playing
segments.summary: John started on guitar in the Bechet band about 1916, took up banjo around 1924, and could pick and strum at once.

segments.title: John leaves with Armstrong; Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: Eddie recalls John leaving for Chicago when Joe Oliver sent for Louis, then praises a cornetist's high-register playing.

segments.title: Eddie subbing for the ailing Simon
segments.summary: Eddie played Simon's jobs while Simon was sick, advertising the band from the truck.

segments.title: How Simon started on bass
segments.summary: Simon made his own bass from a box, their father got him a bass a year later, and neighbourhood boys played penny parties.

segments.title: Simon and John in Kid Rene, Celestin and Ridgley bands
segments.summary: Simon went from Buddy to Kid Rene to Celestin's Tuxedo band, while John was assistant manager and later sided with Ridgley after the split.

segments.title: Simon goes to New York and the Oliver band
segments.summary: Paul Barbarin got Simon to New York with the Blue Rhythm Boys, before John; Simon later toured with the Oliver band led by Paul.

segments.title: Eddie's own sitting in; Ridgley's funeral; purpose of the interview
segments.summary: Eddie sat in for Simon for three months, took calls for Ridgley, and they talk about the band split and Ridgley's funeral.

segments.title: Bunk Johnson and the three trumpeters
segments.summary: Eddie describes Keppard, Joe Oliver and Bunk as his father's trumpeters, and Bunk's sweet style learned from Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Father's band, musicians and halls
segments.summary: Keppard played with his father before Oliver; Eddie names other musicians around, Richard Payne, Louis Nelson, and halls his father played.

segments.title: Father called Billy Moran; brother Lawrence
segments.summary: Outsiders misnamed Billy Marrero as Moran; the sons corrected the name; Russell says he knew Lawrence since 1942.

segments.title: John's death in New York in 1942
segments.summary: Russell recalls hearing from Red Allen that John worked at a drug store in New York; John died in an accident in 1942.

segments.title: Simon's missed chance with Noble Sissle
segments.summary: Lawrence got the best breaks; Simon could have gone overseas with Noble Sissle swapping with a French bassist.

segments.title: Simon's death in 1935 and last job on Streckfus boat
segments.summary: Simon died November 28, 1935; he fell ill about 1933 on a Streckfus boat and was put off in St. Paul after his last job with Fate Marable.

segments.title: Rehearsals and red bean dinners at father's house
segments.summary: Rehearsals at the house drew crowds of white and colored neighbours, and his father cooked red beans for musicians every Monday.

segments.title: Friendliness of old days; musicians carrying instruments
segments.summary: Eddie and Russell contrast the friendlier past with today, and note musicians always took their own instruments to rehearsals.

segments.title: Monday dances and free banquets
segments.summary: Economy Hall-type Monday dances, and society banquets with free food, ham and beer where Eddie got friends in.

segments.title: Bowing, fingering and four-string bass
segments.summary: How older bassists bowed and plucked with two fingers, got calluses, preferred four strings, and learned chords.

segments.title: Other bassists: Jim Little and Albert Morgan
segments.summary: Eddie names Jim Little and Albert Morgan, whom Simon taught, and notes Sam Morgan's rule against letting others sit in.

segments.title: Jimmy Brown, Old Man Kimball and Johnny Prudhomme
segments.summary: Eddie compares older bassists Jimmy Brown, Kimball and the rough-style Prudhomme with his father.

segments.title: Wooden Joe and closing
segments.summary: Eddie mentions Wooden Joe and Lawrence, who played with many bands for over 30 years; the interview ends.
